summary:
RotaSmart is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers explore crop rotation options using NASA Earth observation data. Changing rainfall, rising heat and soil degradation make choosing the next crop increasingly uncertain, and many farmers lack accessible evidence to guide that choice.

The user selects a location on an interactive map, and the app retrieves monthly temperature and precipitation for 2005–2024 from NASA POWER, plus soil properties from SoilGrids. It then calculates reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56), an aridity index, and a 0–100 viability index with drought, heat-stress, erosivity and frost risk indicators. Eight predefined rotations, such as maize → beans → cover crop, are ranked according to the farmer’s own priorities: water, income, risk, soil and labor. Users can also test scenarios with less rainfall or higher temperatures.

Developed with a focus on Huila, Colombia, RotaSmart turns climate and soil data into clear, explainable comparisons that support soil health and resilience. It is a support tool, not a replacement for agronomists or farmers’ own knowledge.
details:
What it does and how it works. RotaSmart is a progressive web app in English and Spanish. The user searches for a place or clicks on an interactive 3D globe or 2D map. The app queries the NASA POWER API (monthly temperature and precipitation, 2005–2024) and the ISRIC SoilGrids API (clay, sand, organic carbon, pH and cation exchange capacity). All analysis runs in the browser using project-defined rules, with FAO-56 guidance for evapotranspiration.

The results include:

- A 0–100 viability index with four factors (water, temperature, soil, risk) and the main limiting factors.

- Climate indicators: mean, maximum and minimum temperature, annual precipitation, reference evapotranspiration and aridity index.

- An annual-cycle chart and 2005–2024 trends per decade.

- Risk bars for drought, heat stress, erosivity and frost.

- Soil properties, marked as coming from SoilGrids or from an estimate.

The app ranks eight predefined rotations, built from ten crop and cover options (maize, beans, cassava, sorghum, coffee, plantain, rice, cacao, cover crop and pasture). The ranking uses five adjustable priorities: water, income, risk, soil and labor. Users can also run what-if scenarios by changing rainfall and temperature.

Benefits. The tool gives farmers and agronomists a clear, transparent way to compare options. Every result comes from visible rules and open data, with no black box and no AI service called at runtime. It highlights practices that support soil health, such as legumes and cover crops, and it is bilingual.

Intended impact: We want to help farmers and agronomists start decisions with evidence about water, heat and soil, so rotations can protect soils, use water better and adapt to changing conditions. Our next steps are to validate the tool with farmers and agronomists in Huila, and to integrate SMAP soil moisture, MODIS vegetation, IMERG precipitation and SRTM terrain. We evaluated these four NASA products but they are not yet part of the analysis.

Tools and technologies: There is no hardware component.

- Software: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Leaflet, D3 Geo, TopoJSON, Zustand, TanStack Query, i18next, Vite PWA and Vitest. It is hosted on Vercel and released under the MIT license.

- Data and services: NASA POWER, SoilGrids, NASA GIBS, Esri World Imagery, EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless, OpenStreetMap, OpenFreeMap, Nominatim, BigDataCloud and geoBoundaries.

- AI tools used during development are declared in the AI section of this form.

Creativity: We combine NASA climate data with global soil data in a single point-and-click experience. Farmers can re-rank rotations by their own priorities and test climate scenarios on the spot. The map falls back through several imagery providers so it keeps working if one fails, and the explainable rule-based approach keeps every result traceable.

Factors we considered.

- The viability index is a guide for open-air, rainfed cultivation, not a yield prediction.

- The risk percentages are model indices, not statistical probabilities.

- Crop characteristics come from FAO references plus prototype assumptions, so not every value has an individual source.

- The rotation sequences are exploratory, and those with perennial crops need agronomic interpretation.

- Global datasets have limited spatial resolution.

- Local validation by farmers and agronomists is essential.

- We documented the licenses and attributions of all data and libraries in CREDITS.md
